definition: An online experiment that assigns traffic to alternative systems and compares outcomes. Marketplace interactions can require more careful experimental units than individual requests.
A rule assigning a response, such as a click or conversion, to a particular earlier impression or click, including the eligible time window.
Area under the receiver operating characteristic curve. For fixed scores, it equals the chance a random positive outranks a random negative, counting ties as half.
When an event or feature value became accessible to the scoring system. It can be later than the time the event occurred.
A group of training examples processed together. B denotes the number of examples in a batch.
The advertiser's offer per billable event, such as a click. It is distinct from a product's price.
An error score for a binary label y and predicted probability p: −[y ln(p) + (1−y) ln(1−p)]. Uses the natural logarithm.
A logical value, either true or false. Often used for masks.
Agreement between predicted probabilities and observed frequencies on the population being evaluated.
An item being considered for recommendation or ad delivery.
A value that identifies a category or entity rather than measuring a quantity. Item IDs and device classes are examples.
Training in which a prediction at a sequence position sees only its allowed earlier context, not future targets.
A recorded interaction with a displayed item. Training labels need explicit rules for valid clicks, attribution, and duplicate events.
Join vectors end to end to make one longer vector.
The chance of an event given specified information. P(A | B) means the probability of A given B.
Information about the current opportunity, such as device, surface, time, and query.
A downstream outcome such as a purchase or signup. The exact action and attribution rule must be specified.
Cost per click. An advertising payment arrangement in which a valid click is the billable event.
Comma-separated values, a text format for tables. Readers must preserve ID strings, missing values, and types deliberately.
Click-through rate. In this guide's binary impression setting: impressions with at least one valid attributed click divided by eligible impressions.
Conversion rate. Its denominator must be stated: clicked impressions, all impressions, or another defined eligible population.
A specification of each field's meaning, type, units, allowed values, missing-value handling, and role.
Using information during training or evaluation that would not be available for the real prediction, such as the outcome being predicted.
Removing duplicate copies of the same event without merging distinct legitimate events.
The quantity used as the divisor in a rate. Clicks per impression and conversions per click have different denominators.
Here, a numerical measurement supplied as a floating-point value. More generally, dense describes an array whose representation is not mostly omitted or zero.
Deep Interest Network, an Alibaba model that weights historical behaviors according to their relevance to a candidate. Basic weighted pooling alone does not capture order.
Multiply matching coordinates of two equal-length vectors and add the products. For [1,2] and [3,4], the result is 1×3 + 2×4 = 11.
A learned vector of numbers representing an entity or category.
A model parameter array whose rows are vectors selected by categorical indices. A shared vocabulary does not by itself imply a shared embedding table.
A transformation or model that turns an input, such as text, an image, or an ID, into a numerical representation.
Converting raw feature values into a defined numerical representation.
One pass through the training examples. Training can make multiple passes.
Measuring a trained model on data not used for its parameter updates.
Information the model is allowed to use to make a prediction.
Mapping values into a fixed number of integer buckets. Different values can collide in the same bucket.
The model influences which items receive exposure; those exposures generate outcomes that influence later training.
Learning parameters or preprocessing statistics from training data.
A commonly used 32-bit floating-point numerical type.
Interactions before the prediction cutoff. Its event order, availability rule, truncation, padding, and masks must be documented.
A logged showing of an item under a stated exposure definition. Logging an impression does not prove the person paid attention.
An item from another example in a batch used as a contrasting candidate for the current user or context.
An integer used to select a vocabulary entry or embedding row. Its size does not measure the importance or magnitude of an ID.
Weighting a retained example by the reciprocal of its inclusion probability, under a specified sampling design.
The entity being recommended: an ad, product, video, article, song, or other candidate.
Combining records from tables using a specified relationship, such as a shared item or impression identifier.
A text format with named fields, objects, lists, numbers, booleans, and null values.
The observed training target. It is separated from prediction inputs.
Mapping distinct categorical values to integer indices. The fitted mapping and unknown-value behavior must be preserved.
The point at which the target window and required log-arrival allowance have completed under the chosen policy.
An indicator that a particular target is valid and should contribute to the corresponding training loss.
Training on a group of candidates belonging to one request, with labels or preferences interpreted within that group.
Binary cross-entropy averaged over examples, possibly with defined weights.
A numerical measure of prediction error that the training procedure tries to reduce.
An array indicating which entries or labels are valid; padded entries must not act as real events.
The sum of values divided by their count; an average.
Bookkeeping such as event IDs, timestamps, and schema versions. Metadata is not automatically a model feature.
An unavailable value, distinct from a measured zero. A default plus a missing indicator can preserve the distinction.
A model trained to predict multiple targets, such as click and conversion, using separate target definitions and validity masks.
The inverse of raising the number e (approximately 2.718) to a power. Written ln; used in the binary cross-entropy formula.
Normalized discounted cumulative gain for the first K items: relevance with greater weight near the top, divided by an ideal ordering's score. Exact gain and discount formulas must be specified.
A label-0 row under a specified outcome rule. In retrieval, a sampled negative is a contrast, not necessarily an observed rejection.
A model made of layers of adjustable weighted computations and nonlinear functions.
A transformation whose output is not simply a constant times its input plus a constant; neural networks use such functions to learn more complex relationships.
Transforming numerical values to a useful scale. The transformation and any fitted statistics must be consistent across training and serving.
A vector with one position per vocabulary entry: 1 for the observed value and 0 everywhere else. An embedding lookup typically uses the equivalent compact integer index.
An experiment using live traffic to compare system behavior and outcomes.
A value absent from a fitted vocabulary. Often abbreviated OOV and mapped to an unknown bucket or handled with hashing.
Adding placeholders to make differently sized lists fit a batch representation. Placeholders are excluded using a mask or length.
Training on a preference comparison between two candidates under a shared context.
Adjustable numbers learned by the model, including weights and embedding vectors.
A typed, column-oriented file format for table data, with support for nested and list-valued columns.
A predicted probability of the joint click-and-conversion event for an impression context.
Predicted click probability for the specified impression context and target definition.
Predicted conversion probability. State whether it is conditional on a click or on an impression.
Selecting feature versions that were valid and available at the prediction cutoff.
Training on one candidate's target at a time. Its individual scores can later be used to rank multiple candidates.
Combining multiple vectors into one summary, such as by a sum, average, or weighted sum.
Observed behavior changes with where an item is displayed, in addition to its relevance.
A label-1 row under a specified outcome rule; in retrieval, an interaction treated as relevant under the training objective.
The time the scoring decision is made. It can precede the time an impression is displayed or logged.
The information defining what is being requested. In retrieval it can include user history and context, not just typed search text.
Scoring and ordering a set of candidate items.
Of all items defined as relevant, the fraction appearing among the first K retrieved results.
A model that updates a running summary as it processes successive events.
A running summary updated as a model processes successive events.
An opportunity at which the system is asked to choose recommendations or ads.
Selecting a manageable candidate set from a much larger catalog.
The probability q that an eligible row is retained by a sampling procedure.
A multiplier determining a row's contribution to the training or evaluation calculation.
The defined structure, field names, types, and semantics of records.
Observed examples differ systematically from the population of interest, for example because only previously shown items have response labels.
Running a trained model on live inputs to produce predictions. Also called inference in this setting.
The dimensions of an array. B × 5 means B rows, each with five entries.
A categorical field whose conceptual one-hot vector is mostly zeros. An embedding model typically receives its compact integer index.
A measurement of how widely values vary around their mean, commonly used when scaling numerical features.
The page, feed, placement, or other product location where an item may be shown.
A numerical array with a shape and data type. A vector is one-dimensional; a matrix has two dimensions.
Held-out examples used for a final assessment after model and configuration choices.
A discrete unit used by a text model, such as a word or part of a word.
Keeping only a specified part of a list, such as the most recent L events.
Separate models produce user/context and candidate vectors. A compatibility function such as a dot product supplies a retrieval score.
Coordinated Universal Time, a worldwide time reference. Z at the end of a timestamp means UTC.
Held-out examples used to compare settings or model versions before final evaluation.
An ordered list of numbers, such as an embedding.
A conversion attributed to an impression without requiring a matching click.
A defined set of categories and the mapping from each to an index.
Multiply each value or vector by its assigned weight and add the results.
A specified time interval, with a documented starting event and inclusive or exclusive endpoints.
